title: Cornell to collaborate on Genesis Mission project to advance quantum computing with AI
excerpt: As part of the ASQC project, College of Arts & Sciences researcher Eun-Ah Kim will develop machine-learning tools for quantum error correction, simulation and neutral-atom quantum systems.
content:
Cornell will participate in a multi-institution collaboration that has received $12 million from the U.S. Department of Energy to advance quantum computing through the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). 

The project, Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing (ASQC), is one of 12 Phase II awards announced October 9 under the Genesis Mission, which aims to integrate the world’s best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation.

Eun-Ah Kim, Hans A. Bethe Professor in the College of Arts and Sciences, is a co-investigator; the project’s principal investigator is Harvard Professor Mikhail Lukin, co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative. Other collaborators on this project, which is administered by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research division of the Department of Energy, include researchers from MIT and the national laboratories at Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley, and Sandia, as well as QuEra Computing, NVIDIA, and Anthropic.

Kim’s group will lead machine-learning work at two points in the pipeline that connects a scientific question to the hardware. The first is compilation: the group will develop a reinforcement-learning compiler that translates a quantum algorithm into the sequence of atom movements and gate operations that a reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computer carries out. 

Read the full story on the College of Arts and Sciences website.
